This study included three independent experiments, each conducted with a separate set of animals. The 1
design and timeline for each experiment are illustrated in Figure 1. Animals were allocated to the 2
experimental groups using block randomization, ensuring balance across presumed sex and home tank 3
origin. Because zebrafish sex cannot be confirmed without gonadal inspection, group allocation was 4
counterbalanced based on external sex characteristics at the time of assignment. To minimize potential 5
biases, the order of behavioral testing was determined using block randomization, with the sequence of 6
randomized blocks generated via random.org, taking into account the test apparatuses to ensure even 7
distribution across treatment conditions. The experimental unit in all analyses was a single animal, with 8
each fish contributing one independent data point to the statistical comparisons. Both the experimenters 9
conducting the behavioral assessments and those responsible for transferring the animals to the test 10
apparatus were blinded to group allocation. 11
Experiment I 12
This experiment investigated the behavioral effects of repeated ketamine exposure at different 13
concentrations. A total of 128 adult zebrafish were randomly assigned to one of four treatment groups (n 14
= 32): control (17 females, 15 males), ketamine 10 mg/L (16 females, 16 males), ketamine 20 mg/L (15 15
females, 17 males), and ketamine 40 mg/L (16 females, 16 males). Missing data in the analysis reflect 16
animal mortality as detailed in the “Statistical analysis” section. Animals received a 20-minute exposure to 17
their assigned treatment once per day from experimental days 1 to 5. For each session, fish were 18
transferred in groups of four to beakers containing 400 mL of the appropriate solution. After the washout 19
period on day 6 (no handling or exposure), a final treatment was administered on day 7. This administration 20
schedule was informed by prior research in mice, which demonstrated behavioral sensitization following 21
five consecutive days of ketamine exposure and a subsequent 48 -hours washout period [27]. Following 22
each exposure, animals were returned to their respective home tanks. Behavioral testing included both 23
the social preference test (SPT) and the open tank test (OTT), conducted in sequence on days 1, 5, and 24
7 immediately after drug exposure. This experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that repeated 25
exposure to ketamine reduces social interaction (as measured by time spent in the interaction zone during 26
the SPT) and increases rotations in the OTT. 27
Experiment II 28
Building on the findings from Experiment I, the 40 mg/L ketamine concentration was selected for further 29
investigation in Experiment II. This experiment evaluated whether behavioral changes induced by 30
ketamine persist after treatment ends, comparing the effects of a single exposure to those of repeated 31
administration. A total of 48 adult zebrafish were randomly assigned to one of three treatment groups (n = 32
16): control (11 females, 5 males), single exposure (7 females, 9 males), and repeated exposure (7 33
females, 9 males). Animals in the repeated group received a 20 -minute exposure to 40 mg/L ketamine 34
once daily from experimental days 1 to 5. The single exposure group was treated with water from days 1 35
to 4 and exposed to 40 mg/L ketamine only on day 5. Control animals were exposed to water throughout 36
the same period. For each exposure session, fish were transferred in groups of four to beakers containing 37
400 mL of the assigned solution. On day 6, animals remained in their home tanks without intervention. 38
Behavioral testing was carried out on day 7, 48 hours after the final exposure. All animals were evaluated 39
in both the SPT and the OTT, in that order. This experiment was designed to test the hypothesis that 40
repeated ketamine exposure induces sustained behavioral alterations as compared to a single exposure. 41

Behavioral tests 10
The SPT and OTT were conducted sequentially to assess behavioral outcomes. Testing took place during 11
the light phase, between 7:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. Animals were recorded from the front view during the 12
SPT and from above during the OTT. Behavioral data were analyzed using ANY-maze® tracking software 13
(version 7.20; Wood Dale, IL, USA). All researchers involved in analyzing the recordings were blinded to 14
group allocation. 15
Social preference test 16
The SPT was used to assess social affiliation in zebrafish [18, 19]. After treatment, each animal was 17
individually placed in a rectangular tank (30 × 10 × 15 cm) positioned between two adjacent tanks (15 × 18
10 × 13 cm each). One side tank contained a group of 10 conspecifics (social stimulus), while the other 19
was left empty (neutral stimulus). All tanks were filled with water under housing conditions to a height of 20
10 cm. The location of the social stimulus (left or right) was alternated across subjects to control for side 21
preference. Water in the setup was replaced between tests. For analysis, the test tank was virtually divided 22
lengthwise into three equal zones: the interaction zone (nearest to the social stimulus), the neutral zone 23
(nearest to the empty tank), and a central intermediate zone. Video recordings lasted 7 minutes, consisting 24
of a 2-minute habituation period followed by 5 minutes of data collection. The primary outcome was time 25
spent in the interaction zone. Additional variables included total distance traveled, maximum speed, 26
number of line crossings, percentage of distance traveled in the interaction zone, and time spent immobile. 27
Open tank test 28
The OTT was conducted immediately after the SPT to evaluate locomotor activity and stereotyped 29
swimming behavior [18]. Each fish was placed in the center of a circular white arena (24 cm in diameter, 30
8 cm high) filled with 2 cm of water under standard conditions. Recordings were captured from an overhead 31
view for a 5 -minute session. The arena was refilled with clean water between trials. For behavioral 32
analysis, the arena was virtually divided into two zones: a center zone (12 cm in diameter) and a peripheral 33
zone. The primary variable of interest was the number of rotations, which served as a marker of repetitive 34
or stereotyped movement. Additional outcomes included total distance traveled, maximum speed, time 35
spent in the center zone, percentage of distance traveled in the center, absolute turn angle, and time spent 36
immobile. 37

groups (n = 32 each), the design had sufficient power (1 -β = 0.88, α = 0.05) to detect a minimum effect 43
size of d = 0.79. Since most of the observed effect sizes exceeded this threshold, the study was adequately 44
powered to detect the effects identified in pairwise comparisons. No outliers were excluded. Six animals 45

Deviations from registered protocols 17
In Experiment I, the preregistered sample size was 48 animals per group (total = 192), but data collection 18
was stopped after 32 animals per group due to consistent results and larger -than-expected effects. The 19
planned analysis involved a two -way ANOVA with treatment group and experimental day as factors. 20
However, because individual animals could not be reliably tracked across days, each day was analyzed 21
independently using one-way ANOVA to avoid inflating the sample size. Additionally, "percent distance in 22
the interaction zone" and "percent distance in the center" were not preregistered outcomes but were 23
included post hoc in Experiment I for consistency with Experiments II and III. In Experiments II and III, 24
although 32 animals per group were planned, testing was halted after one batch (16 per group) due to a 25
lack of apparent treatment effects and to reduce unnecessary animal use, in accordance with the 3Rs 26
principle [35]. Across all experiments, immobility time was analyzed using Kruskal –Wallis followed by 27
Dunn's test instead of ANOVA, as this outcome violated parametric assumptions. 28
RESULTS 29
Experiment I 30
Ketamine administration led to consistent, concentration -dependent behavioral changes across tests. In 31
the SPT, all concentrations reduced time spent in the interaction zone and percent distance in the 32
interaction zone, indicating decreased social preference. At the same time, ketamine increased total 33
distance traveled, maximum speed, and number of line crossings, reflecting a pattern of hyperlocomotion. 34
In the OTT, ketamine also increased number of rotations, distance traveled, and maximum speed, 35
especially at higher concentrations, while the lower concentration increased time spent in the center and 36
percent distance in the center, an anxiolytic -like response typically interpreted as reduced thigmotaxis in 37
an unfamiliar environment. Subgroup analyses revealed no significant differences across testing days for 38
any outcome, suggesting that repeated ketamine exposure did not result in behavioral sensitization. The 39
following sections provide a more detailed account of these results. 40

Experiment II 28
Ketamine administration at 40 mg/L failed to produce sustained behavioral alterations following either 29
acute or repeated exposure. In the SPT, neither a single administration on day 5 nor repeated treatment 30
over 5 consecutive days affected time spent in the interaction zone, percent distance in the interaction 31

immobile. Likewise, in the OTT, no significant effects were observed for number of rotations, distance 33
traveled, time spent in the center, percent distance in the center, absolute turn angle, or time immobile. A 34

hour washout indicates that neither acute nor repeated ketamine exposure at this concentration produced 37
sustained effects. The following sections provide a more detailed account of these results. 38

DISCUSSION 25
The present findings reinforce the potential of zebrafish as a translational model for investigating 26
schizophrenia pathophysiology and screening early -stage antipsychotic candidates, while also showing 27
relevant differences following repeated ketamine exposure as compared to rodents. Literature reviews 28
highlight discrepancies regarding the effects of NMDA antagonists on social and locomotor parameters in 29
zebrafish, often reflecting variation in compound type, dosing protocols, and behavioral assays [1]. In our 30
study, ketamine induced acute, concentration-dependent behavioral alterations in adult zebrafish that were 31
robust and reproducible. In the SPT, ketamine reduced social interaction and increased locomotor activity 32
across all concentrations, while in the OTT it led to more selective effects, including transient increases in 33
rotational behavior and exploratory movement. Despite repeated exposures, no behavioral sensitization 34
emerged, and ketamine-induced changes dissipated following a 48 -hour washout in both 5 - and 14-day 35
protocols. If anything, the OTT findings from Experiment I may point to a potential tolerance effect, as 36
certain behaviors observed on day 1 diminished over subsequent experimental days. However, it remains 37
unclear whether this reflects a true drug tolerance effect or merely results from repeated testing. These 38
results suggest that, under the exposure conditions used here, ketamine's effects are reversible and 39
restricted to the acute phase. Although no persistent alterations were observed, we cannot rule out the 40
possibility that zebrafish might display chronic or progressive phenotypes under alternative experimental 41
designs. 42
Experiment I revealed a clear, concentration-dependent profile of behavioral alterations following ketamine 43
exposure, consistent with schizophrenia -relevant phenotypes. In the SPT, zebrafish showed a robust 44
decrease in social preference across all concentrations, indicated by reduced time and percent distance 45
in the interaction zone. This phenotype parallels the social withdrawal modeled as a negative symptom in 46
rodent studies and is consistent with effects of NMDA receptor antagonists in mammals [36–41]. Alongside 47

reduced social interaction, ketamine produced hyperlocomotion, evidenced by increased distance 1
traveled, swimming speed, and zone crossings. Increased locomotor activity following NMDA receptor 2
antagonism has been widely used as a behavioral readout for the positive symptom dimension of 3
schizophrenia in animal models [2, 42, 43]. These behavioral changes are in line with findings from other 4
NMDA antagonists in zebrafish, which similarly induce both social withdrawal and hyperlocomotion [18, 5
19, 44 –47]. Together, the results highlight the reproducibility and sensitivity of the SPT for detecting 6
schizophrenia-relevant phenotypes in this model. 7
The OTT revealed a more selective profile. Rotational behavior, often interpreted as a marker of stereotypy 8
or repetitive movement, increased transiently at higher concentrations but was not sustained beyond early 9
sessions. Similar increases in rotational behavior have also been reported in previous studies of ketamine 10
exposure, indicating a reproducible effect on repetitive motor activity [21, 22, 48]. Absolute turn angle 11
remained unaffected, and ketamine's impact on general locomotor outcomes in the OTT was milder than 12
in the SPT, emphasizing the influence of test context. Previous findings indicate that NMDA antagonist -13
induced hyperlocomotion is modulated by environmental novelty, with stronger effects typically observed 14
in unfamiliar settings or in response to novel stimuli [18, 46]. In our study, hyperlocomotion following 15
ketamine exposure was greater in the SPT compared to the OTT, likely due to the contextual salience of 16
the task, in which the animal is placed adjacent to a compartment containing ten conspecifics that may 17
enhance arousal or motivational drive. Since the OTT was always conducted after the SPT, we cannot 18
rule out the possibility that this difference reflects a testing order effect. However, prior experiments using 19
MK-801 in which SPT and OTT were conducted in separate groups of animals rather than sequentially in 20
the same individuals still revealed hyperlocomotion in the SPT but no change in distance traveled in the 21
OTT, suggesting that the SPT may be inherently more sensitive to detecting locomotor alterations [18]. 22
Similarly, studies using ketamine in the novel tank test, a context involving only exposure to a new arena, 23
have also failed to detect hyperlocomotion, further supporting the idea that the expression of this 24
phenotype is highly dependent on the salience of the testing environment [22, 49]. 25
At the lowest concentration (10 mg/L), ketamine elicited an anxiolytic -like response, reflected by greater 26
center time and distance in the OTT. Other studies using ketamine have also reported anxiolytic -like 27
effects, but typically at higher concentrations than those tested here (20–60 mg/L), particularly in the novel 28
tank test and light-dark test [20, 22]. However, these findings require further characterization, as ketamine-29
induced changes in locomotor activity may confound anxiety-related outcomes. In rodents, ketamine has 30
also been shown to produce anxiolytic - or antidepressant -like effects [50 –52], though some studies 31
suggest this may only emerge in animals previously exposed to stress protocols [53, 54]. Whether a similar 32
stress-dependent effect exists in zebrafish remains to be tested. 33
Unlike the study that inspired Experiment I [27], repeated ketamine exposure did not induce behavioral 34
sensitization. Instead, responses remained consistent across test days, contrasting with rodent models 35
where repeated NMDA receptor blockade frequently produces progressively amplified behavioral effects 36
[26, 28, 55 –57]. This is in line with previous zebrafish research showing no evidence of tolerance or 37
sensitization in circling behavior following five days of ketamine exposure, suggesting a stable behavioral 38
profile over repeated administrations [48]. 39
Experiments II and III assessed behavioral persistence after 5-day and 14-day exposure schedules, each 40
followed by a 48 -hour washout. In both cases, zebrafish behavior returned to baseline, with no lasting 41
effects observed in social interaction, locomotion, or repetitive activity. A small reduction in maximum 42
speed following 5-day exposure and increase in immobility was detected following 14 -day exposure, but 43
overall, the results suggest that ketamine's behavioral effects are transient in adult zebrafish under these 44
conditions. 45
Studies examining the sustained effects of ketamine in zebrafish remain scarce. One study using the novel 46
tank test reported that repeated exposure to ketamine (40 mg/L for seven days, with testing 24 hours later) 47

of rotational behavior compared to our approach. In our study, rotations were assessed in the OTT using 3

rodent models, where repeated ketamine exposure often results in sustained disruptions in behavior [25, 5
58]. 6
Zebrafish show sustained neurogenesis and regenerative ability in the central nervous system from early 7
development through adulthood [59 –62]. This may have contributed to the lack of sensitization or long -8
term behavioral effects observed in our study, as the animals may recover from repeated acute exposures. 9
Supporting this, other studies have also found no lasting damage when ketamine was administered during 10
early developmental stages [63]. In rodents, repeated exposure to NMDA receptor antagonists like 11
ketamine causes lasting impairment in cortical inhibitory circuits by triggering a redox -sensitive pathway. 12
Repeated dosing increases IL-6 levels in the brain, which activates NADPH oxidase ( Nox2) and leads to 13
oxidative stress that disrupts the function of parvalbumin-expressing interneurons [23, 64]. These effects 14
do not occur after a single exposure and appear only after repeated challenges. While reversible in adult 15
rodents, they become permanent when the exposure occurs during development [64, 65]. Zebrafish may 16
be less sensitive to these changes, potentially requiring more frequent or intense exposure to produce 17
similar long-term effects. 18
The NMDA receptor is highly conserved across vertebrate species, including zebrafish [45, 66, 67]. 19
Subunit composition, binding affinity, and overall receptor function are similar enough to support 20
comparable acute effects across species. Therefore, differences in behavioral outcomes are unlikely to 21
result from receptor pharmacology alone. One possible explanation involves species-specific differences 22
in ketamine metabolism. Although zebrafish express cytochrome P450 enzymes involved in drug 23
processing [68, 69], little is known about how ketamine is metabolized in this species. It is unclear how 24
quickly the drug is metabolized, which metabolites are generated, and whether any of them contribute to 25
behavioral effects. These factors may influence the limited duration of responses observed in this species. 26
Investigating ketamine's pharmacokinetics in zebrafish will be important for interpreting its behavioral 27
impact and for evaluating the model's relevance to other systems. 28
The findings presented here highlight the utility of zebrafish for modeling behavioral changes induced by 29
NMDA receptor antagonists. However, to improve the translational relevance of this model, future studies 30
should include pharmacological validation using clinically effective antipsychotic drugs and incorporate 31
neurochemical or physiological analyses to clarify underlying mechanisms. Expanding the behavioral 32
assessments to cover cognitive and affective domains, alongside systematic variation in exposure 33
conditions such as dosing schedules, developmental timing, and environmental context, will allow for a 34
more comprehensive evaluation of induced phenotypes. 35
The lack of sensitization or lasting behavioral effects likely reflects the specific exposure protocols used, 36
rather than an inherent limitation of the zebrafish model. Variations in exposure timing, duration, dose, or 37
the inclusion of environmental stressors may be necessary to produce more persistent effects. The 38
zebrafish offers significant experimental flexibility, and its potential to model chronic or progressive features 39
of psychiatric disorders warrants further investigation. 40
In summary, ketamine induced robust, context -dependent, and reversible behavioral alterations in adult 41
zebrafish that parallel core symptom dimensions of schizophrenia. The use of complementary behavioral 42
assays enabled a multidimensional assessment of drug effects, reinforcing the model's potential for acute 43
psychotomimetic screening. While the current exposure protocols did not produce sensitization or long -44
lasting behavioral changes, these findings establish a strong foundation for future studies aimed at 45
optimizing the zebrafish model for translational neuropsychiatric research. With further refinement and 46
validation, zebrafish hold considerable promise as a scalable platform for mechanistic discovery and early-47

DISCUSSÃO


A

presente

tese

teve

como

objetivo

principal

avaliar

os

efeitos

de

antagonistas

do

receptor

NMDA

sobre

o

comportamento

social

em

animais

de

laboratório

e

discutir

sua

relevância

para

modelar

fenótipos

relacionados

aos

sintomas

negativos

da

esquizofrenia.

Os

dois

estudos

desenvolvidos

indicam

que

esses

fármacos

induzem

alterações

sociais

detectáveis

em

organismos

modelo.

A

revisão

sistemática

e

meta-análise

mostrou

que

o

antagonismo

NMDA

reduz

medidas

de

interação

social

e

de

preferência

social

em

diferentes

espécies.

O

estudo

experimental,

por

sua

vez,

mostrou

que

a

cetamina

reduz

medidas

sociais

em

peixe-zebra

adulto.

No

entanto,

esse

efeito

ocorreu

junto

a

alterações

locomotoras,

não

se

intensificou

após

exposições

repetidas,

indicando

ausência

de

sensibilização

comportamental,

e

não

persistiu

após

um

período

sem

exposição.

Em

conjunto,

esses

achados

sustentam

a

relevância

dos

antagonistas

NMDA

para

investigar

alterações

sociais

em

modelos

animais,

mas

também

mostram

que

esses

desfechos

precisam

ser

interpretados

considerando

o

teste

utilizado

e

comportamentos

com

potencial

confundidor

da

medida

social.

Esse

ponto

é

particularmente

relevante

porque

os

sintomas

negativos

da

esquizofrenia

permanecem

entre

os

mais

difíceis

de

tratar

e

de

modelar

experimentalmente.

Embora

antipsicóticos

sejam

eficazes

para

reduzir

sintomas

positivos,

seus

efeitos

sobre

sintomas

negativos

primários,

funcionamento

social

e

cognição

são

limitados

(Correll;

Schooler,

2020;

Fusar-Poli

et

al.,

2015;

Huhn

et

al.,

2019;

McCutcheon;

Keefe;

McGuire,

2023).

Assim,

modelos

animais

voltados

a

esses

domínios

devem

ser

interpretados

com

cautela.

Medidas

de

comportamento

social

em

animais

são

úteis

porque

permitem

quantificar

respostas

observáveis,

como

aproximação,

permanência

próxima

a

coespecíficos,

interação

direta

ou

coesão

entre

indivíduos

(Toth;

Neumann,

2013;

Wilson;

Koenig,

2014).

No

entanto,

essas

medidas

não

correspondem

diretamente

à

associalidade,

avolia

ou

anedonia

observadas

em

pacientes.

Elas

funcionam

como

aproximações

experimentais

de

componentes

do

comportamento

social,

e

não

como

equivalentes

completos

dos

sintomas

negativos.


No

primeiro

estudo,

a

síntese

da

literatura

mostrou

que

MK-801,

cetamina

e

PCP

estão

associados

à

redução

do

comportamento

social

em

animais

de

laboratório.

Esse

achado

sustenta

a

ideia

de

que

a

hipofunção

NMDA

interfere

em

145

processos

comportamentais

relevantes

para

o

domínio

social.

Ao

mesmo

tempo,

a

magnitude

dos

efeitos

variou

significativamente

entre

estudos,

paradigmas

e

espécies,

indicando

que

este

fenômeno

não

é

uniforme.

Essa

interpretação

é

reforçada

pelo

fato

de

que

a

literatura

também

inclui

estudos

sem

alteração

detectável

ou

até

com

aumento

de

medidas

de

sociabilidade

após

a

exposição

a

antagonistas

NMDA.

Parte

dessa

variação

parece

estar

relacionada

à

intensidade

da

exposição

farmacológica,

já

que

a

meta-regressão

mostrou

associação

entre

maior

dose

cumulativa

de

antagonistas

NMDA

e

maior

redução

da

interação

social

em

roedores.

Essa

relação,

no

entanto,

não

foi

observada

de

forma

clara

para

preferência

social.

Essa

heterogeneidade

era

esperada,

considerando

que

os

modelos

baseados

em

antagonistas

NMDA

diferem

quanto

ao

fármaco

utilizado,

dose,

via

de

administração,

duração

da

exposição,

intervalo

entre

tratamento

e

teste,

idade

dos

animais

e

tipo

de

desfecho

social

avaliado

(Benvenutti

et

al.,

2022;

Lee;

Zhou,

2019;

Neill

et

al.,

2010).

Além

dessas

diferenças

experimentais,

a

revisão

também

evidenciou

limitações

no

relato

metodológico

de

parte

da

literatura

pré-clínica.

Informações

sobre

randomização,

cegamento,

cálculo

amostral,

definição

da

unidade

experimental

e

manejo

de

dados

nem

sempre

são

descritas

de

forma

suficiente

nos

estudos

com

animais.

Também

foram

observados

indícios

de

efeitos

de

estudos

pequenos,

compatíveis

com

viés

de

publicação

ou

superestimação

de

efeitos

em

estudos

com

menor

precisão,

sobretudo

nas

análises

de

preferência

social.

Esse

ponto

é

importante

porque

dificulta

avaliar

até

que

ponto

a

variação

entre

os

estudos

reflete

diferenças

biológicas

reais,

diferenças

de

protocolo

ou

limitações

de

desenho

e

relato

experimental.

A

análise

dos

desfechos

locomotores

reforça

essa

interpretação.

Em

muitos

testes

sociais,

o

animal

precisa

explorar

o

aparato,

deslocar-se

até

o

estímulo

social

e

distribuir

seu

tempo

entre

zonas

com

ou

sem

coespecíficos.

Por

isso,

alterações

motoras

podem

modificar

medidas

sociais.

Essa

limitação

já

havia

sido

apontada

em

discussões

sobre

testes

de

sociabilidade

em

roedores,

nos

quais

mudanças

na

exploração,

ansiedade,

resposta

à

novidade

ou

atividade

locomotora

podem

interferir

no

tempo

de

interação

ou

de

permanência

em

uma

zona

social

(Toth;

Neumann,

2013;

Wilson;

Koenig,

2014;

Yang;

Silverman;

Crawley,

2011).

Esse

problema

também

foi

observado

nos

resultados

da

revisão

sistemática

e

meta-análise.

Os

efeitos

sociais

dos

antagonistas

NMDA

frequentemente

apareceram

junto

a

alterações

locomotoras.

146

Esse

aspecto

também

é

importante

para

interpretar

os

efeitos

de

antipsicóticos

nos

modelos

animais.

Em

estudos

pré-clínicos,

a

prevenção

ou

reversão

de

alterações

sociais

por

antipsicóticos

costuma

ser

usada

como

evidência

de

validade

preditiva.

No

entanto,

essa

interpretação

deve

ser

limitada

pelo

que

se

observa

na

clínica.

Se

os

antipsicóticos

disponíveis

têm

efeito

pequeno

ou

inconsistente

sobre

sintomas

negativos

primários,

a

reversão

de

um

déficit

social

em

animais

não

deve

ser

automaticamente

entendida

como

evidência

de

restauração

de

uma

função

social

equivalente

à

humana

(Correll;

Schooler,

2020;

Fusar-Poli

et

al.,

2015;

Krause

et

al.,

2018).

No

primeiro

estudo,

a

melhora

de

medidas

sociais

em

animais

tratados

com

antipsicóticos

apareceu

acompanhada

por

mudanças

locomotoras.

Isso

sugere

que

parte

do

efeito

pode

refletir

alteração

da

atividade

geral,

sedação

ou

redistribuição

do

tempo

no

aparato

e

não

necessariamente

uma

melhora

seletiva

da

sociabilidade.

O

segundo

estudo

caracterizou

os

efeitos

da

cetamina

em

peixes-zebra

adultos

e

ajudou

a

avaliar

essa

questão

em

uma

espécie

complementar

aos

roedores.

A

cetamina

reduziu

medidas

sociais,

aumentou

a

atividade

locomotora

no

teste

de

preferência

social

e

alterou

o

padrão

de

nado

no

teste

de

tanque

aberto.

Esses

resultados

indicam

que

o

peixe-zebra

adulto

é

sensível

aos

efeitos

comportamentais

agudos

da

hipofunção

de

receptores

NMDA.

Esse

achado

está

de

acordo

com

a

literatura

que

descreve

o

peixe-zebra

como

um

modelo

vertebrado

com

sistemas

neuroquímicos

conservados

e

repertórios

comportamentais

quantificáveis

de

interesse

para

a

esquizofrenia

e

outros

transtornos

psiquiátricos

(Benvenutti

et

al.,

2022;

Kalueff;

Stewart;

Gerlai,

2014;

Langova

et

al.,

2020;

Stewart

et

al.,

2014).

No

entanto,

como

a

redução

das

medidas

sociais

ocorreu

junto

ao

aumento

da

locomoção,

os

dados

não

sustentam

uma

interpretação

simples

de

déficit

social

seletivo.

Esse

achado

corrobora

aqueles

encontrados

na

meta-análise.

A

ausência

de

sensibilização

comportamental

após

exposições

repetidas

à

cetamina

e

a

ausência

de

efeitos

persistentes

após

o

período

sem

exposição

também

são

achados

relevantes.

Em

roedores,

protocolos

repetidos

com

antagonistas

NMDA

são

frequentemente

utilizados

para

investigar

alterações

mais

duradouras,

incluindo

mudanças

comportamentais

que

permanecem

após

efeito

agudo

do

fármaco

(Frohlich;

Van

Horn,

2014;

Lee;

Zhou,

2019;

Neill

et

al.,

2010).

Esse

padrão,

porém,

não

foi

observado

em

peixe-zebra

adulto

nas

condições

testadas.

Isso

não

invalida

o

modelo,

mas

delimita

sua

utilidade.

Os

resultados

147

sustentam

o

uso

do

peixe-zebra

para

investigar

respostas

agudas

aos

antagonistas

NMDA.

Por

outro

lado,

os

protocolos

empregados

não

forneceram

evidência

de

que

a

exposição

repetida

produza

sensibilização

ou

alterações

persistentes

após

48

horas

sem

tratamento.

Essa

diferença

em

relação

a

parte

da

literatura

em

roedores

pode

ter

várias

explicações.

Diferenças

entre

espécies,

vias

de

administração,

absorção

por

imersão,

metabolismo,

concentração

efetiva

no

sistema

nervoso

e

características

dos

testes

comportamentais

podem

influenciar

os

resultados.

Outro

aspecto

a

considerar

é

que

o

sistema

nervoso

central

do

peixe-zebra

adulto

apresenta

capacidade

neurogênica

e

regenerativa

mais

ampla

do

que

a

observada

em

mamíferos,

com

múltiplas

zonas

neurogênicas

distribuídas

pelo

encéfalo

e

respostas

de

reparo

mais

robustas

após

lesão

(Ghaddar

et

al.,

2021;

Kizil,

2018;

Kizil

et

al.,

2012).

Embora

essa

característica

não

explique

diretamente

os

resultados

observados,

pois

não

foi

avaliada

neste

estudo,

ela

pode

ser

relevante

para

interpretar

diferenças

entre

espécies

na

persistência

e

reversibilidade

de

alterações

comportamentais

após

insultos

ao

sistema

nervoso

central.

Além

disso,

o

comportamento

social

do

peixe-zebra

é

estruturado

de

forma

diferente

do

comportamento

social

de

roedores.

A

espécie

apresenta

uma

tendência

robusta

a

se

aproximar

de

coespecíficos

e

formar

cardumes,

característica

que

sustenta

o

uso

de

testes

de

preferência

social

em

peixe-zebra.

Nesse

tipo

de

paradigma,

porém,

a

resposta

social

é

inferida

a

partir

da

distribuição

espacial

do

animal

na

arena

e

da

permanência

próxima

ao

estímulo

social,

que

permanece

fisicamente

separado

por

barreiras

transparentes

(Barba-Escobedo;

Gould,

2012;

Miller;

Gerlai,

2007).

Por

isso,

alterações

no

padrão

de

nado,

na

exploração

do

ambiente

ou

na

locomoção

podem

interferir

na

medida

social

obtida

no

teste.

Estudos

futuros

poderiam

combinar

esse

tipo

de

abordagem

com

medidas

de

coesão

social.

Essa

combinação

ajudaria

a

avaliar

se

os

efeitos

observados

refletem

uma

alteração

mais

ampla

do

comportamento

social

ou

se

dependem

do

tipo

de

paradigma

utilizado.

Considerados

em

conjunto,

os

dois

estudos

reforçam

a

utilidade

dos

modelos

baseados

em

antagonismo

NMDA

para

investigar

alterações

sociais

associadas

a

fenótipos

relacionados

à

esquizofrenia.

Essa

utilidade

se

apoia

na

relevância

da

hipofunção

NMDA

para

a

fisiopatologia

proposta

da

esquizofrenia,

uma

vez

que

alterações

nesse

sistema

podem

afetar

o

equilíbrio

entre

neurotransmissão

glutamatérgica,

GABAérgica

e

dopaminérgica

em

circuitos

envolvidos

no

transtorno

148

(Coyle,

2012;

Gonzalez-Burgos;

Lewis,

2012;

Howes;

Shatalina,

2022;

Moghaddam;

Javitt,

2012).

Ao

mesmo

tempo,

os

achados

reforçam

que

esses

modelos

não

devem

ser

interpretados

como

reproduções

completas

dos

sintomas

negativos.


A

coexistência

de

alterações

sociais

e

locomotoras

limita

a

leitura

desses

modelos

como

medidas

seletivas

de

sintomas

negativos

e

exige

cautela

ao

usar

a

reversão

por

antipsicóticos

como

evidência

de

validade

preditiva.

Em

peixes-zebra

adultos,

a

cetamina

produziu

efeitos

agudos,

mas

não

persistentes,

sobre

medidas

sociais

e

locomotoras,

sugerindo

maior

utilidade

do

modelo

para

avaliar

respostas

agudas

à

hipofunção

NMDA

do

que

alterações

sustentadas.

Em

conjunto,

esses

resultados

reforçam

que

dados

de

interação

ou

preferência

social

devem

ser

analisados

junto

a

possíveis

confundidores

comportamentais,

especialmente

locomoção.

Também

indicam

que

diferenças

entre

espécies,

protocolos

e

formas

de

mensurar

o

comportamento

social

precisam

ser

consideradas

antes

de

extrapolar

os

achados

pré-clínicos

para

sintomas

negativos

ou

para

a

eficácia

de

intervenções

farmacológicas.

CONCLUSÕES


A

presente

tese

mostrou

que

antagonistas

do

receptor

NMDA

reduzem

medidas

de

comportamento

social

em

animais

de

laboratório.

A

revisão

sistemática

e

meta-análise

indicou

que

esse

efeito

ocorre

em

paradigmas

de

interação

social

e

de

preferência

social,

embora

com

variação

entre

estudos,

espécies,

fármacos

e

protocolos

experimentais.

Os

resultados

também

mostraram

que

alterações

sociais

induzidas

por

antagonistas

NMDA

devem

ser

interpretadas

junto

a

outros

parâmetros

comportamentais.

Em

parte

da

literatura

pré-clínica,

os

efeitos

sobre

interação

ou

preferência

social

ocorrem

em

paralelo

a

alterações

locomotoras,

o

que

limita

a

interpretação

desses

desfechos

como

medidas

seletivas

de

sociabilidade

ou

como

equivalentes

diretos

de

sintomas

negativos.

A

análise

dos

efeitos

de

antipsicóticos

reforçou

essa

necessidade

de

cautela.

Embora

esses

fármacos

possam

atenuar

alterações

sociais

induzidas

por

antagonistas

NMDA

em

modelos

animais,

esses

efeitos

frequentemente

aparecem

acompanhados

por

mudanças

locomotoras.

Assim,

a

reversão

de

déficits

sociais

por

antipsicóticos

não

deve

ser

interpretada,

isoladamente,

como

evidência

de

validade

preditiva

para

sintomas

negativos.

No

estudo

experimental,

a

cetamina

induziu

alterações

sociais

e

locomotoras

agudas

em

peixe-zebra

adulto.

Esses

efeitos

incluíram

redução

de

medidas

sociais,

aumento

da

atividade

locomotora

no

teste

de

preferência

social

e

alterações

no

padrão

de

nado

no

teste

de

tanque

aberto.

No

entanto,

não

foram

observadas

evidências

de

sensibilização

comportamental

após

exposições

repetidas

nem

persistência

dos

efeitos

após

48

horas

sem

exposição.

Em

conjunto,

os

achados

apoiam

o

uso

do

peixe-zebra

como

modelo

complementar

para

investigar

respostas

comportamentais

agudas

à

hipofunção

NMDA.

Ao

mesmo

tempo,

indicam

que

sua

utilidade

depende

do

desfecho

avaliado,

do

protocolo

de

exposição

e

da

análise

conjunta

de

possíveis

confundidores

comportamentais,

especialmente

locomoção.

Assim,

esta

tese

contribui

para

o

refinamento

da

interpretação

de

desfechos

sociais

em

modelos

animais

de

esquizofrenia.

Os

resultados

sustentam

que

modelos

baseados

em

antagonismo

NMDA

são

úteis

para

investigar

alterações

sociais

em

animais,

mas

que

sua

relevância

translacional

depende

da

forma

como

esses

efeitos

são

medidos,

controlados

e

relacionados

aos

domínios

clínicos

da

esquizofrenia.

Modelos

animais

baseados

na

hipofunção

de

receptores

N
-metil-D-aspartato

(NMDA)

são

amplamente

utilizados

para

investigar

fenótipos

comportamentais

relacionados

à

esquizofrenia

e

para

a

triagem

de

candidatos

a

fármacos

com

potencial

antipsicótico.

No

entanto,

a

interpretação

desses

modelos

é

dificultada

pela

heterogeneidade

metodológica,

por

potenciais

confundidores

comportamentais

e

por

limitações

relacionadas

à

validade

interna

e

externa

dos

achados.

Esta

tese

teve

como

objetivo

avaliar

os

efeitos

de

antagonistas

do

receptor

NMDA

sobre

o

comportamento

social

em

animais

de

laboratório

e

discutir

sua

relevância

para

modelar

fenótipos

relacionados

aos

sintomas

negativos

da

esquizofrenia.

Para

isso,

foram

desenvolvidos

dois

estudos

complementares.

No

primeiro

estudo,

realizou-se

uma

revisão

sistemática

e

meta-análise

de

estudos

pré-clínicos

sobre

os

efeitos

de

dizocilpina

(MK-801),

cetamina

e

fenciclidina

(PCP)

sobre

interação

e

preferência

social

em

ratos,

camundongos

e

peixes-zebra.

Foram

incluídos

264

estudos

identificados

nas

bases

Embase,

PubMed

e

Web

of

Science.

Os

dados

foram

sintetizados

por

modelos

de

efeitos

aleatórios

multinível.

A

síntese

dos

dados

indicou

que

antagonistas

do

receptor

NMDA

reduzem

o

comportamento

social,

embora

a

magnitude

e

a

consistência

desses

efeitos

variem

conforme

o

paradigma

experimental,

com

alta

heterogeneidade

e

indícios

de

efeitos

de

estudos

pequenos,

especialmente

nas

análises

de

preferência

social.

Antipsicóticos

clinicamente

aprovados

atenuaram

alterações

sociais

induzidas

por

antagonistas

NMDA;

entretanto,

esses

efeitos

frequentemente

ocorreram

junto

a

mudanças

na

locomoção,

dificultando

sua

interpretação

como

restauração

seletiva

do

comportamento

social.

No

segundo

estudo,

foram

avaliados

os

efeitos

da

cetamina

em

peixes-zebra

adultos.

Os

animais

foram

expostos

à

cetamina

por

imersão

durante

20

minutos.

No

primeiro

experimento,

as

concentrações

de

10,

20

e

40

mg/L

foram

avaliadas

após

exposição

aguda,

após

cinco

dias

de

exposição

repetida

e

após

reexposição

no

dia

7,

precedida

por

48

horas

sem

tratamento.

Nos

experimentos

seguintes,

a

concentração

de

40

mg/L

foi

utilizada

para

investigar

se

os

efeitos

persistiam

48

horas

após

protocolos

de

5

ou

14

dias

de

exposição,

sem

nova

administração

antes

dos

testes.

Os

comportamentos

foram

avaliados

nos

testes

de

preferência

social

e

de

tanque

aberto.

A

cetamina

reduziu

o

comportamento

social,

aumentou

a

atividade

locomotora

no

teste

de

preferência

social

e

induziu

alterações

no

padrão

de

nado

no

teste

de

tanque

aberto.

Esses

efeitos,

porém,

não

se

intensificaram

após

exposições

repetidas,

indicando

ausência

de

sensibilização

comportamental,

nem

persistiram

após

o

período

sem

exposição,

revelando

uma

diferença

significativa

em

relação

ao

que

se

observa

em

roedores.

Em

conjunto,

os

resultados

indicam

que

antagonistas

do

receptor

NMDA

induzem

alterações

sociais

em

modelos

animais,

mas

também

evidenciam

limitações

relevantes

para

a

interpretação

translacional

desses

fenótipos.

Esta

tese

contribui

para

uma

avaliação

crítica

da

utilidade

e

dos

limites

de

modelos

baseados

em

antagonismo

NMDA

no

estudo

de

sintomas

negativos

da

esquizofrenia.

animais.

ABSTRACT



Schizophrenia

is

a

complex

psychiatric

disorder

characterized

by

positive,

negative,

and

cognitive

symptoms.

Although

antipsychotics

are

effective

in

controlling

positive

symptoms,

negative

symptoms,

such

as

social

impairments,

remain

an

important

unmet

clinical

need.

Animal

models

based

on

N
-methyl-D-aspartate

(NMDA)

receptor

hypofunction

are

widely

used

to

investigate

schizophrenia-related

behavioral

phenotypes

and

to

screen

drug

candidates

with

potential

antipsychotic

effects.

However,

the

interpretation

of

these

models

is

hampered

by

methodological

heterogeneity,

potential

behavioral

confounders,

and

limitations

related

to

the

internal

and

external

validity

of

the

findings.

This

thesis

aimed

to

evaluate

the

effects

of

NMDA

receptor

antagonists

on

social

behavior

in

laboratory

animals

and

to

discuss

their

relevance

for

modeling

phenotypes

related

to

the

negative

symptoms

of

schizophrenia.

To

this

end,

two

complementary

studies

were

conducted.

In

the

first

study,

a

systematic

review

and

meta-analysis

of

preclinical

studies

on

the

effects

of

dizocilpine

(MK-801),

ketamine,

and

phencyclidine

(PCP)

on

social

interaction

and

social

preference

in

rats,

mice,

and

zebrafish

was

conducted.

A

total

of

264

studies

identified

in

Embase,

PubMed,

and

Web

of

Science

were

included.

Data

were

synthesized

using

multilevel

random-effects

models.

The

data

synthesis

indicated

that

NMDA

receptor

antagonists

reduce

social

behavior,

although

the

magnitude

and

consistency

of

these

effects

vary

according

to

the

experimental

paradigm,

with

high

heterogeneity

and

evidence

of

small-study

effects,

especially

in

the

social

preference

analyses.

Clinically

approved

antipsychotics

attenuated

social

alterations

induced

by

NMDA

antagonists;

however,

these

effects

frequently

occurred

alongside

changes

in

locomotion,

making

it

difficult

to

interpret

them

as

selective

restoration

of

social

behavior.

In

the

second

study,

the

effects

of

ketamine

were

evaluated

in

adult

zebrafish.

Animals

were

exposed

to

ketamine

by

immersion

for

20

minutes.

In

the

first

experiment,

concentrations

of

10,

20,

and

40

mg/L

were

evaluated

after

acute

exposure,

after

five

days

of

repeated

exposure,

and

after

re-exposure

on

day

7,

preceded

by

48

hours

without

treatment.

In

the

following

experiments,

the

40

mg/L

concentration

was

used

to

investigate

whether

the

effects

persisted

48

hours

after

5-

or

14-day

exposure

protocols,

without

a

new

administration

before

testing.

Behaviors

were

assessed

in

the

social

preference

and

open

tank

tests.

Ketamine

reduced

social

behavior,

increased

locomotor

activity

in

the

social

preference

test,

and

induced

alterations

in

swimming

patterns

in

the

open

tank

test.

However,

these

effects

did

not

intensify

after

repeated

exposures,

indicating

the

absence

of

behavioral

sensitization,

nor

did

they

persist

after

the

period

without

exposure,

revealing

a

significant

difference

compared

to

what

is

observed

in

rodents.

Taken

together,

the

results

indicate

that

NMDA

receptor

antagonists

induce

social

alterations

in

animal

models,

but

also

highlight

relevant

limitations

for

the

translational

interpretation

of

these

phenotypes.

This

thesis

contributes

to

a

critical

evaluation

of

the

utility

and

limitations

of

models

based

on

NMDA

antagonism

in

the

study

of

negative

symptoms

of

schizophrenia.


Keywords:

schizophrenia;

negative

symptoms;

social

behavior;

NMDA

receptor

antagonists;

ketamine;

zebrafish;

animal

models.

INTRODUÇÃO



1.1

ESQUIZOFRENIA


A

esquizofrenia

é

um

transtorno

psiquiátrico

complexo

e

heterogêneo,

marcado

por

início

relativamente

precoce

e

por

prejuízos

que

podem

se

estender

a

diferentes

dimensões

do

cotidiano.

A

primeira

apresentação

clínica

costuma

aparecer

no

fim

da

adolescência

ou

no

início

da

vida

adulta,

com

um

pico

de

incidência

entre

os

20

e

24

anos

(Zhan;

Wang;

Shen,

2025).

Em

muitos

casos,

porém,

as

mudanças

começam

antes

do

primeiro

episódio

psicótico.

Esse

período

prodrômico

pode

envolver

declínio

cognitivo

e

alterações

graduais

no

desempenho

ocupacional

e

interpessoal,

contribuindo

para

prejuízos

funcionais

ainda

nas

fases

iniciais

do

transtorno

(Leucht

et

al.,

2025).

Embora

afete

uma

parcela

pequena

da

população,

sua

relevância

epidemiológica

é

expressiva

considerando

que

estimativas

recentes

apontam

uma

prevalência

ao

longo

da

vida

entre

0,4%

e

0,62%

na

população

geral

(Leucht

et

al.,

2025;

Zhang

et

al.,

2026).

Segundo

as

estimativas

do

Global

Burden

of

Disease

de

2019

e

2021,

o

número

de

pessoas

vivendo

com

esquizofrenia

aumentou

de

cerca

de

14

milhões

em

1990

para

mais

de

23

milhões

(Solmi

et

al.,

2023;

Zhan;

Wang;

Shen,

2025).

Os

anos

de

vida

ajustados

por

incapacidade

(DALYs,

do

inglês

disability-adjusted

life

years
)

também

aumentaram,

passando

de

valores

próximos

de

9

milhões

para

cerca

de

15

milhões

no

mesmo

período

(Solmi

et

al.,

2023;

Zhan;

Wang;

Shen,

2025).

Ambas

as

análises

indicam

relativa

estabilidade

das

estimativas

padronizadas

por

idade

em

escala

global,

sugerindo

que

o

crescimento

da

carga

se

relaciona

principalmente

a

mudanças

demográficas,

como

o

crescimento

populacional

e

o

envelhecimento,

além

de

diferenças

regionais

na

identificação

dos

casos

(Solmi

et

al.,

2023;

Zhan;

Wang;

Shen,

2025).

Embora

a

esquizofrenia

seja

mais

frequentemente

lembrada

pelos

sintomas

psicóticos,

suas

consequências

se

estendem

para

além

da

fase

aguda

do

transtorno.

Em

uma

meta-análise

sobre

a

recuperação

após

o

primeiro

episódio

de

psicose,

apenas

cerca

de

20%

dos

indivíduos

avaliados

alcançaram

a

recuperação

clínica

(Hansen

et

al.,

2023).

Essa

baixa

frequência

de

recuperação

global

não

se

restringe

à

persistência

de

sintomas

psicóticos.

Mesmo

após

a

remissão

parcial

de

9

delírios

e

alucinações,

a

melhora

clínica

nem

sempre

se

traduz

em

recuperação

funcional.

Muitos

indivíduos

continuam

a

apresentar

prejuízos

cognitivos

e

dificuldades

de

funcionamento

social

e

ocupacional,

que

são

pouco

responsivos

aos

tratamentos

disponíveis

(Leucht

et

al.,

2025).

A

inserção

no

mercado

de

trabalho

também

é

frequentemente

comprometida,

com

taxas

de

emprego

consistentemente

reduzidas

(Holm

et

al.,

2021;

Marwaha;

Johnson,

2004).

Além

dos

prejuízos

funcionais,

a

esquizofrenia

está

associada

à

mortalidade

prematura.

Em

uma

revisão

sistemática

e

meta-análise

que

incluiu

135

estudos,

pessoas

com

esquizofrenia

apresentaram

risco

de

mortalidade

por

todas

as

causas

2,52

vezes

maior

em

comparação

com

grupos

sem

o

transtorno,

além

de

uma

redução

estimada

de

15

a

20

anos

na

expectativa

de

vida

(Correll

et

al.,

2022).

De

forma

convergente,

uma

meta-análise

mais

ampla

sobre

transtornos

mentais

estimou

15,37

anos

de

vida

potencialmente

perdidos

devido

a

este

transtorno,

em

comparação

com

a

população

geral

(Chan

et

al.,

2023).

Esses

dados

indicam

que

o

prejuízo

funcional

e

a

mortalidade

prematura

são

componentes

centrais

da

carga

clínica

e

social

associada

a

este

transtorno

mental.

As

evidências

disponíveis

apontam

para

uma

etiologia

multifatorial,

resultante

da

interação

entre

predisposição

genética

e

exposição

a

fatores

ambientais.

Embora

estudos

com

gêmeos

indiquem

uma

contribuição

genética

importante

para

o

transtorno,

essa

vulnerabilidade,

por

si

só,

não

é

suficiente

para

explicar

sua

ocorrência

(Hilker

et

al.,

2018;

Sullivan;

Kendler;

Neale,

2003).

A

literatura

também

associa

o

transtorno

a

fatores

presentes

em

diferentes

fases

do

desenvolvimento,

incluindo

complicações

obstétricas

e

infecções

maternas

(Davies

et

al.,

2020),

bem

como

adversidades

na

infância

(Varese

et

al.,

2012).

Outros

fatores

ambientais

e

sociais,

como

residência

em

áreas

urbanas,

migração

e

uso

frequente

de

cannabis,

também

são

recorrentes

em

estudos

epidemiológicos

(Henssler

et

al.,

2020;

Marconi

et

al.,

2016;

Vassos

et

al.,

2012).

Esse

conjunto

de

evidências

reforça

a

heterogeneidade

da

esquizofrenia

e

ajuda

a

explicar

a

variabilidade

observada

em

sua

apresentação

clínica.



1.1.1

Apresentação

clínica

10

A

apresentação

varia

consideravelmente

entre

e

ao

longo

do

curso

alterações

comportamento,

na

percepção,

no

na

motivação

e

na

acordo

o

Manual

Diagnóstico

e

da

de

discurso

desorganizado,

comportamento

desorganizado

ou

catatônico

e

sintomas

negativos,

acompanhados

de

comprometimento

funcional

e

de

sinais

contínuos

do

transtorno

por

pelo

menos

seis

meses,

com

pelo

menos

um

mês

de

sintomas

da

fase

ativa

(American

Psychiatric

Association,

2022).

Embora

essa

definição

seja

útil

para

o

diagnóstico

clínico,

a

esquizofrenia

costuma

ser

ABSTRACT
Social withdrawal is a key component of the negative symptom domain of schizophrenia, and
pharmacological blockade of the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) is widely used to model
schizophrenia-relevant phenotypes in animals. However, findings on social behaviour are
inconsistent across paradigms and laboratories. We therefore conducted a systematic review and
meta-analysis to synthesise the effects of dizocilpine, ketamine, and phencyclidine on social
interaction and social preference, to evaluate whether clinically approved antipsychotics modify
these outcomes, and to examine locomotor activity measured within the same social tests to aid
interpretation. We searched Embase, PubMed and Web of Science without language or date
restrictions. Controlled in vivo studies in laboratory animals administering an eligible NMDAR
antagonist and reporting social interaction and/or social preference outcomes were included. Two
reviewers independently screened records, extracted data and assessed risk of bias. Effect sizes
were computed as standardised mean differences and synthesised using correlated multilevel
random-effects models with cluster-robust variance estimation. In total, 264 studies met the
inclusion criteria. Overall, NMDAR antagonists were associated with reduced social interaction and
reduced social preference relative to controls, although the social preference literature appeared
vulnerable to small-study effects and imprecision. Locomotor activity measured during social
interaction tests tended to be higher following NMDAR antagonists, whereas during social
preference no consistent overall change was observed. In animals exposed to NMDAR
antagonists, antipsychotics increased social behaviour, but these changes commonly co-occurred
with reduced locomotion during social interaction tests, suggesting that improvements in social
measures may partly reflect altered behavioural competition and time allocation rather than
selective restoration of social functioning. Taken together, the evidence supports an overall link
between NMDAR antagonism and reduced social behaviour, but the strength and interpretability of
this signal depend on the paradigm and are constrained by heterogeneity and limitations in
reporting.
Keywords: NMDA receptor antagonists, ketamine, PCP, MK-801, social interaction, social
preference, locomotor activity, antipsychotics, preclinical animal models, schizophrenia.

I. INTRODUCTION
Social withdrawal and impaired social functioning are core components of the negative symptom
domain of schizophrenia and are closely associated with long-term functional disability and
reduced quality of life (Galderisi et al., 2018; Harvey, Strassnig & Silberstein, 2019; Correll &
Schooler, 2020; Mosolov & Yaltonskaya, 2022). In contrast to positive symptoms, which are
responsive to antipsychotic treatment in most patients, negative symptoms demonstrate limited
and inconsistent improvement with currently available pharmacotherapies, with reported benefits
often attributable to changes in secondary negative symptoms (Fusar-Poli et al., 2015; Leucht et
al., 2017; Krause et al., 2018; Correll & Schooler, 2020; Sabe et al., 2021). Social dysfunction,
therefore, remains a persistent clinical problem and an important target for translational research
(Millan et al., 2014; Spark et al., 2022; Howes, Fusar-Poli & Osugo, 2023).
Among the neurobiological hypotheses of schizophrenia, N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDAR)
hypofunction has received substantial empirical support from convergent post-mortem findings
(Vrajová et al., 2010; Weickert et al., 2013; Catts et al., 2016) and pharmacological evidence in
humans (Allen & Young, 1978; Newcomer et al., 1999; Adler et al., 1999; Lahti et al., 2001;
Pomarol-Clotet et al., 2006). Consistent with this framework, NMDAR antagonist-based animal
models using non-competitive antagonists such as dizocilpine (MK-801), ketamine, and
phencyclidine (PCP) are well established in preclinical research, being employed to elicit
behavioural and neurochemical alterations related to the positive, cognitive, and negative
symptoms of schizophrenia (Neill et al., 2010; Frohlich & Van Horn, 2014; Miyamoto & Nitta, 2014;
Lee & Zhou, 2019; Benvenutti et al., 2022; Li et al., 2024).
Although social behaviour has been extensively examined in these models, reported findings
remain inconsistent across the literature, with studies reporting null effects (Becker & Grecksch,
2004; Hanks et al., 2013) and even unexpected increases in sociability (Dunn, Corbett & Fielding,
1989; Jenkins et al., 2008; Rawat et al., 2022). The latter has also been observed in our laboratory,
where acute MK-801 administration increased social behaviour in adult C57BL/6 mice (Giongo et
al., 2023). Social outcomes are measured using heterogeneous paradigms, most commonly free
social interaction and social preference tests (Toth & Neumann, 2013; Wilson & Koenig, 2014).

Social interaction paradigms quantify direct reciprocal behaviours between freely moving
conspecifics (File & Hyde, 1978), whereas social preference paradigms measure approach or
proximity to a constrained social stimulus (Landauer & Balster, 1982; Wee et al., 1995; Haller &
Bakos, 2002; Nadler et al., 2004), also capturing motivational or exploratory components besides
interaction per se. Furthermore, substantial variation exists in apparatus design, outcome
definitions, species, developmental stage, dosing schedules, and administration routes (Neill et al.,
2010; Benvenutti et al., 2022). As a result, it remains unclear to what extent the observed
differences reflect biological effects of NMDAR blockade rather than methodological
inconsistencies.
Interpretation is further complicated by two recurring issues. First, antipsychotics are routinely used
in animal studies to test the pharmacological sensitivity of NMDAR antagonist–induced phenotypes
(Spark et al., 2022), yet clinically available antipsychotics provide little to no benefit for primary
negative symptoms in patients and have a limited impact on their social functioning (Correll &
Schooler, 2020; Howes et al., 2023). For this reason, the apparent normalisation of social
alterations in animals cannot, on its own, be taken as evidence of translational relevance (Hagan &
Jones, 2005; Large, 2007; Wilson & Koenig, 2014). Therefore, it remains crucial to determine
whether the reported antipsychotic effects on social outcomes reflect specific modulation of social
behaviour or instead arise from non-specific changes in arousal, anxiety, or motor output, and to
assess how robust these effects are across species, paradigms, and laboratories. Second,
NMDAR antagonists are also known to cause hyperlocomotion (Lee & Zhou, 2019; Benvenutti et
al., 2022). Locomotor changes can directly influence measures of both reciprocal interaction and
proximity-based social behaviour (Yang, Silverman & Crawley, 2011; Mitchell et al., 2020),
separating social effects from non-specific motor effects is thus not always straightforward.
Beyond heterogeneity in experimental design and insufficient reporting of key methodological
practices, this area of research may also be affected by inadequate handling of non-independent
observations (Sena et al., 2010; Landis et al., 2012; Hirst et al., 2014; Macleod et al., 2015; Wilson
et al., 2023; Townsend et al., 2025). In social behaviour experiments, non-independence can arise
when multiple measurements are obtained from the same animal, when interacting animals within

Although the existing literature suggests that NMDAR antagonists induce social behaviour deficits,
the magnitude, consistency, and moderators of these effects have not been established. A
quantitative synthesis is therefore required to integrate the available evidence, characterise
heterogeneity, evaluate potential sources of bias, and assess the extent to which experimental
factors and pharmacological interventions modulate reported effects (Bahadoran et al., 2020;
Ineichen et al., 2024b). This systematic review and meta-analysis addresses the following
question: what are the effects of NMDAR antagonists on social behaviour in laboratory animals?
Secondary objectives are to evaluate the effects of clinically approved antipsychotics on social
outcomes in NMDAR antagonist–exposed animals and to assess locomotor activity as a control
outcome to aid interpretation of social measures.
II. METHODS
(1) Protocol
The protocol for this systematic review and meta-analysis was registered in the International
Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO, registration number:
CRD42023402129) prior to study screening and data extraction (Gallas-Lopes et al., 2024). The
preregistered protocol specified the research questions, eligibility criteria, search strategy, and
planned analyses.
The primary objective of the review was to evaluate the effects of NMDAR antagonists (MK-801,
ketamine, or PCP) on social behaviour in laboratory animals, with social behaviour operationalised
as social interaction or social preference outcomes. Secondary objectives were to assess the
effects of clinically approved antipsychotics on social behaviour in animals exposed to NMDAR

This review adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
(PRISMA) guidelines (Page et al., 2021a, 2021b). All data and materials associated with this study,
including extracted datasets and analysis code, are publicly available via the Open Science
Framework (OSF) at osf.io/98fau (Gallas-Lopes et al., 2023a) and GitHub at
github.com/matheusglls/NMDA-sb (Gallas-Lopes, 2026).
(2) Study selection
Systematic searches were conducted in Embase, PubMed, and Web of Science on February 25 th,
2023. The search strategy was designed to capture studies evaluating the effects of NMDAR
antagonists on social behaviour in laboratory animals and combined controlled vocabulary and
free-text terms relating to the population (laboratory animals), intervention (NMDAR antagonists),
and outcomes (social interaction and social preference). For the population component, validated
SYRCLE animal filters were used to ensure broad coverage of laboratory animal studies across
species (van der Mierden et al., 2022). No restrictions were applied on language or publication
date. Full database-specific search strategies were preregistered and are available at
https://osf.io/5k2br (Gallas-Lopes et al., 2023b).
Records retrieved from the database searches were exported and imported to Rayyan (Ouzzani et
al., 2016), where duplicate entries were identified and removed using a combination of automated
detection and manual verification. Study selection was carried out in two phases: an initial
screening based on titles and abstracts, followed by a full-text eligibility assessment. In both
phases, each record was evaluated independently by two reviewers, and decisions were made
blinded to the other reviewer’s judgment.
During the title and abstract screening stage, records were excluded only when they clearly failed
to meet eligibility criteria related to study design, population, or intervention. Specifically, studies

(3) Data collection
Data extraction was performed in two sequential stages: an initial qualitative extraction to
characterise study and experimental features, followed by quantitative extraction of outcome data
for meta-analysis. Qualitative and quantitative extractions were conducted following predefined
guides, available at osf.io/98fau/files/k928m and osf.io/98fau/files/bhdp3, respectively. Both stages
were conducted independently by two reviewers using standardised extraction forms developed
before data collection. When discrepancies occurred or when differences between extracted
quantitative values exceeded 10%, reconciliation was performed by a third reviewer who
re-extracted the discrepant information to establish final values.
In the qualitative extraction stage, descriptive information was collected for each experiment,
including publication details, animal characteristics (species, strain, sex, age, or developmental
stage at both induction and outcome assessment), and intervention parameters (NMDAR
antagonist used, dose or concentration, route of administration, frequency and duration of
exposure, and interval between drug administration and behavioural testing). Characteristics of the

appropriate biological unit. For example, when social behaviour was quantified separately for each
animal within interacting pairs, the effective sample size was divided by two to account for
non-independence within dyads.
Experiments conducted in distinct sets of animals within the same study were entered as separate
effect sizes, while dependence among effect sizes from the same study was accounted for using

results obtained exclusively from naive animals. When multiple experiments were conducted
sequentially in the same animals, only data from the first behavioural assessment were retained.

and within the same experimental context as the social behaviour assessment. When outcomes
were assessed at multiple time points within the same experiment, only the earliest
post-intervention time point was considered. Outcomes exclusively assessing social novelty
preference were not considered eligible. When essential quantitative information, such as sample

(4) Risk of bias
Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE’s risk of bias tool for animal studies (Hooijmans et al.,
2014b), with additional domains addressing pseudoreplication and procedural equivalence.
Pseudoreplication refers to the inappropriate treatment of non-independent observations (e.g.,
multiple measurements from the same animal or cage) as independent experimental units, which
can inflate precision and bias effect estimates (Lazic et al., 2018). Procedural equivalence
assesses whether experimental groups were handled identically aside from the intervention (e.g.,
same housing conditions, handling, route of administration, timing, and outcome assessment
procedures), minimising performance and detection bias. Due to pervasive poor reporting in animal
studies, the allocation concealment domain was omitted, as it cannot be objectively evaluated in
most included studies (Hirst et al., 2014). A detailed assessment guide with operational definitions
and decision rules for each domain is publicly available at osf.io/98fau/files/5gkct.
Only experiments and behavioural outcomes relevant to this review were considered when
assigning risk of bias judgments. When a study included more than one eligible experiment or
behavioural test, judgments were made for each relevant experiment and then summarised at the
study level. This summary followed a conservative approach: if any relevant experiment within a
study was judged as high risk in a given domain, the study was classified as high risk for that
domain. Domains included sequence generation, baseline characteristics, random housing,
blinding during the experiment, random outcome assessment, blinding during outcome
assessment, incomplete outcome data, selective outcome reporting, pseudoreplication, and
procedural equivalence. For each domain, risk of bias was rated as low, unclear, or high. An overall
study-level classification was then assigned and dichotomised as low or high, with studies rated as
high overall risk of bias when at least one domain was judged as high risk. All assessments were

(5) Outcome selection and effect size estimation
When more than one outcome assessing the same behavioural domain (social preference, social
interaction, or locomotor activity) was extracted for the same group of animals within an
experiment, only one outcome was selected for inclusion in the meta-analysis. This approach was
adopted to avoid multiple dependent effect sizes arising from the same animals. Outcome selection
followed a predefined hierarchy based on the frequency in which specific outcome types were
reported across studies and on how directly each measure captured the behavioural construct of
interest. Outcomes with different names but assessing the same underlying construct were
grouped and ranked accordingly.
For social preference and social interaction, time-based measures reflecting the absolute duration
of social behaviour were prioritised, as these were the most frequently reported and provided the
most direct quantification of social behaviour. When time-based measures were not available, we
selected the available measure that most directly represented the same construct, prioritising
proportion- or index-based measures of social behaviour. Latency- or distance-based outcomes
(e.g., latency to first contact, distance to the stimulus) were selected only when no other measures
were reported.

Relative, normalised, or derived locomotor measures were included when no absolute locomotor

Effect sizes were calculated as standardised mean differences using the Hedges’ g method, with
corresponding sampling variances estimated using the escalc function of the metafor package in R
(version 4.3.1) (Viechtbauer, 2010). To ensure consistent directionality across outcomes, effect
sizes were reversed when lower values indicated higher levels of social behaviour, such as latency
to first social contact or measures based on inter-individual distance.
The distribution of effect sizes included in the meta-analyses was summarised visually to
characterise the structure of the available evidence. Alluvial plots were used to illustrate how effect
sizes were distributed across key study characteristics and were constructed using the ggalluvial
package (Brunson & Read, 2023). Evidence maps were constructed to summarise the number of
effect sizes and their mean magnitude across combinations of experimental factors, providing an
overview of data density and coverage.
(6) Data synthesis
Meta-analyses were conducted separately for two conceptually distinct domains of social
behaviour: social interaction and social preference. Social interaction paradigms were defined as
those allowing direct physical interaction between two or more conspecifics. In contrast, social
preference paradigms assessed interest in or proximity to a conspecific whose movement or
physical contact was restricted (e.g., wire cages or enclosed compartments). Locomotor activity
outcomes assessed during social behaviour tests were analysed in parallel with each social
domain.
Based on these distinctions and the experimental contrasts of interest, seven independent
meta-analyses were performed:

Effect sizes were synthesised using correlated multilevel random-effects models, in which effect
sizes were nested within experiments and experiments were nested within studies, to properly
account for dependencies. Random intercepts for both study and experiment were included to
capture between-study and within-study variability. Models were fitted using restricted maximum
likelihood estimation. In addition, cluster-robust variance estimation at the study level was applied
to all models using the clubSandwich package (Pustejovsky, Pekofsky & Zhang, 2025), providing
additional protection against residual dependence.
To account for shared control groups and resulting dependency between effect sizes derived from
the same experiment, correlations were modelled using a variance–covariance matrix constructed
with the vcalc function. A within-experiment correlation coefficient (ρ) of 0.5 was assumed.
Heterogeneity was examined to evaluate how much effect sizes varied beyond sampling error.
Cochran’s Q statistic was used to test whether heterogeneity was present. The magnitude of
heterogeneity was quantified using multilevel I² estimates (Nakagawa et al., 2023) and variance

confidence intervals around pooled estimates, prediction intervals were calculated to indicate the
expected range of true effects that might be observed in future studies, incorporating both
sampling error and between-study heterogeneity.
Small-study effects, which may reflect publication bias, were examined using funnel plots and
regression-based methods. Funnel plots were constructed using standard error and the inverse
square root of the total sample size to assess asymmetry (Egger et al., 1997; Sterne et al., 2011;
Zwetsloot et al., 2017). Precision-effect test (PET) and precision-effect estimate with standard error
(PEESE) models were fitted by regressing effect sizes on standard error and sampling variance,
respectively, within the multilevel framework. Following recommended practice, when the PET
indicated evidence of small-study effects (i.e., a significant slope), the PEESE estimate was
interpreted as the primary bias-adjusted effect size; otherwise, the PET estimate was retained
(Stanley, 2008; Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2014). As an additional sensitivity analysis, we performed
a regression using a standard error adjusted for effective sample size. This approach reduces the
artifactual correlation between standardized mean differences and their standard errors, providing
a complementary assessment of small-study effects. Time-lag bias was assessed using
meta-regression with publication year centred around its mean and included as a continuous
moderator (Yang et al., 2023).

effects of NMDAR antagonists on social interaction and social preference varied across key
experimental and biological characteristics and to assess whether these variables explained part of
the between-study heterogeneity. A priori planned categorical moderators included NMDAR
antagonist, species, developmental stage at induction, route of administration, dosing schedule,
sex, and, when applicable, antipsychotic treatment. All moderator models were fitted; however,

(7) Sensitivity analyses
Sensitivity analyses were conducted using the same correlated multilevel random-effects models
with robust variance estimation applied in the primary analyses. First, to assess the robustness of
pooled estimates to the assumed within-experiment correlation used in the variance–covariance
matrix, models were re-estimated using alternative values of ρ across a plausible range (0.0, 0.3,
0.5, and 0.8). Second, to assess the influence of individual studies, leave-one-study-out analyses
were performed by sequentially excluding each study and re-estimating the pooled effect, allowing
evaluation of whether the overall results were disproportionately driven by any single study. Third,
analyses were repeated after excluding studies classified as having high overall risk of bias, to
examine whether conclusions were sensitive to the inclusion of studies with greater methodological
limitations. Consistency between the primary and sensitivity analyses was interpreted as evidence
of robustness.
(8) Deviations from protocol
Some qualitative variables were extracted as prespecified, yet were not analysed because
reporting was unclear or incomplete in most studies. Locomotor activity was initially planned for
extraction whenever reported; however, we ultimately extracted it only when it was measured
during the social test and in the same animals, to better evaluate whether locomotor changes could
confound social outcomes. Locomotion measured in separate apparatuses or in different animals
was therefore not included in our analyses. In addition, the data synthesis approach and risk of

III. RESULTS
Visualisations of the primary and secondary analyses are provided at
matheusglls.github.io/NMDA-sb.
(1) Study selection
A total of 2,261 records were identified through database searches, including Embase (n = 913),
PubMed (n = 708), and Web of Science (n = 640). After the removal of 941 duplicate records,
1,320 records remained and were screened based on titles and abstracts. Of these, 401 records
were excluded, primarily due to study design (n = 204), intervention (n = 183), and population (n =
14) not meeting the eligibility criteria. Consequently, 919 reports were sought for retrieval, of which
8 reports could not be retrieved. The remaining 911 reports underwent full-text assessment for
eligibility. At this stage, 647 reports were excluded for not meeting the following criteria: study
design (n = 147), population (n = 11), intervention (n = 172), comparison (n = 12), outcome of
interest (n = 288), and insufficient or missing data (n = 17). Ultimately, 264 studies met the
inclusion criteria and were included in the quantitative synthesis (Figure 1), including studies in rats
(Rattus spp.), mice (Mus spp.), and zebrafish (Danio rerio). The complete list of included studies is
available at https://osf.io/98fau/files/5qevp.
(2) Risk of bias
Across domains, most studies were judged as having an unclear risk of bias, reflecting widespread
under-reporting of key methodological details in the preclinical literature (Figure 2). This was
particularly evident for domains related to randomisation procedures. Random sequence
generation was judged as unclear in 98% of studies. Similarly, random housing was rated as

of the experimental unit, especially in social interaction paradigms where individual animals within
the same interacting dyad were treated as independent observations. Procedural equivalence was
judged as low risk in 75% of studies, unclear in 13%, and high risk in 12%, indicating that most
studies applied comparable procedures across groups, although methodological concerns
remained in a minority of cases. When summarised across all domains, 55% of studies were
classified as overall low risk of bias and 45% as high risk.

between reviewers, with a Cohen’s kappa of 0.643 and a PABAK of 0.627. Of all ratings, 81.3% (n

disagreement. Critical disagreement, defined as opposing judgments at the extremes of the scale
(low vs high risk), accounted for 4.8% (n = 128) of all ratings.

assessment (0.958); however, corresponding Cohen’s kappa values were moderate (0.538, 0.437,
and 0.333, respectively), likely reflecting the high prevalence of “unclear” ratings in these domains.
Blinding of outcome assessment showed both high observed agreement (0.883) and high
agreement beyond chance (kappa 0.765). Lower levels of agreement were observed for
incomplete outcome data (observed agreement 0.682, kappa 0.439), selective outcome reporting
(observed agreement 0.769, kappa 0.215), pseudoreplication (observed agreement 0.557, kappa
0.245), and procedural equivalence (observed agreement 0.712, kappa 0.179), indicating greater
subjectivity in judging these items.
Study- and domain-level risk of bias assessments are reported in the online resource at
matheusglls.github.io/NMDA-sb/risk_of_bias/rob_and_interrater.html, together with additional

IV. DISCUSSION
Across the included studies, exposure to NMDAR antagonists was associated with reduced social
behaviour overall; however, the robustness of this pattern varied depending on the behavioural
paradigm and on bias diagnostics. In social interaction tests, NMDAR antagonists significantly
reduced social interaction relative to controls, with substantial heterogeneity and wide prediction
intervals; although the effect size was attenuated after adjustment for small-study effects, it
remained statistically significant. For social preference paradigms, the pooled estimate was also
significant, yet this effect was eliminated after bias adjustment, indicating greater sensitivity to
imprecise studies and potential publication bias. Locomotor activity assessed during social
paradigms provided important interpretive context, as antagonists increased activity during social
interaction tests but showed no clear effects during social preference. Finally, clinically approved
antipsychotics were associated with higher social interaction and social preference in animals
exposed to NMDAR antagonists, with reduced locomotion in social interaction paradigms,
indicating that apparent normalisation of social outcomes co-occurred with changes in general
activity.
In this systematic review, we analysed social interaction and social preference as distinct outcome
domains, not only because they operationalise social behaviour in different ways, but also because
the evidence bases underpinning each domain have different profiles. Social interaction outcomes
were drawn from a much larger evidence base and covered a longer publication period (1989 to
2023, median 2013), whereas social preference outcomes came from a smaller and more recent
literature (2009 to 2023, median 2016). Although these differences in publication era and reporting
practices could, in principle, contribute to discrepancies between domains, the time-lag analyses

Both domains were represented across the same species, including rats, mice, and zebrafish, but
